analysis.one_liner: Bans Members of Congress, federal judges, and top officials from trading individual stocks and puts their finances online for the public.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House on June 5, 2025 with 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to four House committees; none has taken it up, and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: STOCK Act 2.0 would ban members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve officials, and their families from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, including through trusts and synthetic workarounds. They would have to divest within 120 days, keep only diversified mutual funds and Treasury securities, and pay a fine of at least 10 percent of the value of anything traded in violation. It would also require officials and their families to report any federal contract, loan, or grant they or their businesses receive, and would force all financial disclosures onto searchable, downloadable public websites.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would get a searchable public record of every lawmaker's and top official's finances, and a government where the people who write laws and regulate markets cannot bet on their own decisions with individual stocks, futures, commodities, or crypto. The ban covers spouses and dependent children and closes loopholes like blind trusts and derivatives that mirror stock positions.

how_it_helps.text: Bans members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve governors and bank presidents, and their spouses and dependent children from holding, buying, or selling any individual security, future, commodity, or cryptocurrency, and bars them from short-selling. [S2]

Requires divestiture within 120 days, applies the ban through trusts and synthetic holdings like options and warrants, and imposes a fine of at least 10 percent of the value of any violating position. [S2]

Requires covered officials and their families to report any application for or receipt of federal money, including loans, contracts, and grants, within 30 to 45 days, with a $5,000 fine for failing to report. [S2]

Requires electronic filing and public websites that let anyone search, sort, and download financial disclosure and transaction data by filer, asset, ticker, and date, with public access through an application programming interface, covering Congress, senior executive officials, federal judges, and Federal Reserve bank officers. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, top executive officials, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve officials, who would have to sell off individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto within 120 days and put the proceeds into diversified funds or Treasury securities. Any wealth managers who run those individual portfolios lose the business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and other top officials

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the existing criminal fine language for late transaction reports with a flat $1,000 fine in each case, a fixed penalty that a large trader could treat as a cost of doing business. [S2]

Covered officials may still hold diversified mutual funds and Treasury securities, so they can keep money fully invested in the broad market, whose direction their own legislative and regulatory work can influence; they are also exempt from bans on securities tied to a spouse's primary employer. [S2]

Enforcement runs entirely through supervising ethics offices, with divestiture-extension requests subject to up to 150 days of extensions, and history suggests these offices enforce disclosure rules unevenly; the bill gives them no new independent investigative staff. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large: it removes the ability of the people who write laws and regulate markets to trade on their own decisions, and it makes their finances searchable online. The cost falls almost entirely on the officials themselves, and even then only on their ability to hold individual securities, since diversified index funds and Treasury bonds remain allowed. The design has real soft spots — a flat $1,000 fine for late transaction reports is weaker than the current criminal-fine language, and ethics offices have enforced disclosure rules unevenly — but the core ban is stronger than the existing STOCK Act, which requires only disclosure, not divestiture.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to four House committees on the same day; months later none of them has taken any action, so there is no vote of any kind.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Min and nine colleagues introduced the bill in the House on June 5, 2025. [S1][S2]
The Speaker referred it to the Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced. [S4]
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no committee report, and no floor vote after the referral. [S4]
Eighteen House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and other covered officials keep the ability to trade individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto under the existing disclosure-only rules, and the wealth managers who run their individual portfolios keep the business. Citizens keep a disclosure system that relies on paper filings and self-reporting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting officials and their wealth managers

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors are House Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; the four committees that received the bill are chaired by Republicans, and no Republican has cosponsored.

industries.industry: Sitting federal officeholders (Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve officials)
industries.note: They would have to divest individual stocks, futures, commodities, and crypto within 120 days and would face fines of at least 10 percent of the value of any violating position, while continuing to be able to hold diversified index funds and Treasuries. Because the bill died in committee, they keep the current disclosure-only regime. [S2][S4]

industries.industry: Wealth managers and brokerages serving elected and appointed officials
industries.note: They would lose the individual-stock portfolios of Members of Congress, justices, and Fed officials, business worth relatively little in dollar terms but politically valuable for firms courting government connections. [S2]

industries.industry: Companies and contractors receiving federal money from officials' family connections
industries.note: The bill does not restrict them, but it forces any covered official whose family or business receives a federal contract, loan, or grant to report it publicly within 45 days, raising the cost of steering federal money to their own circle. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but nothing has happened since the June 5 referral to four committees. A single-member bill with no Republican cosponsors and no committee action has almost no realistic path to a floor vote in this Congress; similar stock-trading ban proposals have repeatedly stalled the same way. The only realistic routes left are a late push attached to must-pass legislation or a new Congress starting from scratch.
